Windows and Linux are not vulnerable.

```
pid.stat('1 && /usr/local/bin/python');
```

This vulnerability is not affected on Node.js environment since Node.js's implementation of RegExp.prototype.toString() backslash-escapes all forward slashes in regular expressions. If serialized data of regular expression objects are used in an environment other than Node.js, it is affected by this vulnerability.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Escape serialized regex content before replacing placeholders**

Regex placeholders are replaced with raw `RegExp#toString()` output here, but the unsafe-character escaping pass already ran earlier on the placeholder-filled JSON string. As a result, regex payloads containing HTML-significant characters or JS line terminators bypass the sanitizer and are emitted directly into the returned JavaScript, which can re-open script-injection risk when this output is embedded into an HTML `<script>` block (the default use case described in this package).

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Do not delete function properties from caller-owned objects**

With `ignoreFunction` enabled, the replacer invokes `deleteFunctions(value)`, and that helper mutates the original object graph by deleting function-valued keys in place. This means a serialization call can silently strip methods from application state (including nested objects) after serialization, causing downstream logic to break in ways unrelated to serialization and diverging from `JSON.stringify`-style non-mutating behavior.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Sanitize linkback URL before injecting profile HTML**

In `Comments.addLinkbackToArticle`, the `url` value is concatenated directly into an `<a href=...>` HTML string, but that same field is persisted from `req.body.url` in `publishArticle` with no escaping/validation. A publisher (or any actor able to submit that endpoint) can store a crafted value such as a `javascript:` URL or quote-breaking payload, which then renders in post profile metadata and can execute as stored XSS for users viewing the topic.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Use a consistent page size when fetching paginated posts**

The start index uses `pagination * 10`, but the end index uses `9 + pagination * 9`, so page 0 returns 10 items while later pages return progressively fewer (9, 8, ...). For threads with more than one page, this creates missing/skipped comments and breaks the front-end load-more assumptions in `ghost.js/general.js` that each additional page contains up to 10 posts.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

cve_explanation: In the npm package semantic-release before version 17.2.3, secrets that would normally be masked by `semantic-release` can be accidentally disclosed if they contain characters that become encoded when included in a URL. Secrets that do not contain characters that become encoded when included in a URL are already masked properly. The issue is fixed in version 17.2.3.

detected_issues.explanation:
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Encode secret before escaping the encoded redaction pattern**

The encoded alternative is currently generated as `encodeURI(escapeRegExp(env[envVar]))`, which escapes regex metacharacters first and then URI-encodes those backslashes, producing a pattern that does not match the actual URI-encoded secret. When a token contains regex-significant characters (for example `+`, `^`, `{`, `}`), the plain-text value may be masked but its encoded form can still appear in logs, undermining this function’s secret-redaction guarantee.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

This is criticizing the quality/completeness of the fix implementation, not detecting the original CVE. cve_explanation: Fast-csv is an npm package for parsing and formatting CSVs or any other delimited value file in node. In fast-cvs before version 4.3.6 there is a possible ReDoS vulnerability (Regular Expression Denial of Service) when using ignoreEmpty option when parsing. This has been patched in `v4.3.6` You will only be affected by this if you use the `ignoreEmpty` parsing option. **<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve CR at chunk boundary for comment lines**

On the next chunk, the leading `\n` is then parsed as a standalone empty row, which corrupts row output for streamed CRLF inputs with comments. `RowParser` already guards this exact boundary case for data rows, so comment handling should keep the partial line buffered until `\n` arrives.

When `ignoreEmpty` is enabled, `parseRow` runs `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP` against user-provided row content, and this pattern has nested optional/repeating pieces (`\s*` with `(?:,\s*(?:''|"")?\s*)*`) that exhibit super-linear backtracking on long non-matching strings. A crafted oversized CSV line can therefore tie up CPU during parsing, creating a ReDoS path in streaming workloads that parse untrusted input.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve column boundaries in ignoreEmpty check**

The empty-row filter checks `EMPTY_ROW_REGEXP.test(row.join(''))`, which strips delimiters between parsed columns and can misclassify non-empty rows as empty. For example, the valid row `"",","` parses to `['', ',']`, `join('')` becomes `","`, and the regex matches it as empty, so the row is silently dropped when `ignoreEmpty` is true.

cve_explanation: In affected versions of dojo (NPM package), the deepCopy method is vulnerable to Prototype Pollution. An attacker manipulates these attributes to overwrite, or pollute, a JavaScript application object prototype of the base object by injecting other values. This has been patched in versions 1.12.8, 1.13.7, 1.14.6, 1.15.3 and 1.16.2

This mutates caller input (for example, query/body arrays containing nullable values) and can serialize incorrect payloads downstream (e.g., `null` becoming `[object Object]`). Add a null/type guard before recursing so nullable array elements are copied as-is.

The `QUOTED` expression lets a backslash match both alternation branches (`\\[\x00-\x7f]` and `[^"]...`), so `parseHeader()` can spend exponential time in `EXT_LIST.test(header)` on malformed quoted params (for example, a missing closing quote after many backslashes). Because `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` is peer-controlled during the handshake, this creates a practical ReDoS vector that can block the Node.js event loop for seconds with relatively short input.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reset NOTOKEN state before each value test**

`NOTOKEN` is declared with the global flag and reused via `NOTOKEN.test(value)` while serializing multiple params, which makes `lastIndex` leak between calls. This causes false negatives after a prior match, so later values that require quoting can be emitted unquoted (e.g. serializing `{b:'x,y', c:'p,q'}` produces `c=p,q`), yielding invalid `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` headers and negotiation failures.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.
